Work from that copy: read whole and as stored, this file pulls every session toward the same shape.

how_to_read: 1. Deal first: python3 <SKILL>/scripts/deal.py rare-clouds-haiku.metadump.json, then read the dealt copy it names for every step below (write-backs go to this file).
2. Read the head: the first 34 lines hold manifest, essence and routing (Read limit=34, or jq '{manifest, essence, routing}' rare-clouds-haiku.metadump.json).
3. Pick the route for your job and run its jq: jq '<routing[i].jq>' rare-clouds-haiku.metadump.json
4. Also pull the anti-keywords and review prompts (checks) for your scope: jq '.anti_keywords, .checks' rare-clouds-haiku.metadump.json
5. Look up any term (lowercase): jq '.index["<term>"]' rare-clouds-haiku.metadump.json  -> hits give id + path; not_meant lists senses to avoid.
6. Grep works too: every entry is one line, so grep -n '<word>' rare-clouds-haiku.metadump.json returns whole entries.

essence.one_sentence: What makes a rare cloud interesting is the conditions the sky shows (cold, a standing wave, shear, a storm base, a short window of light), so its rarity can sit in what the eye sees rather than in the word rare.
essence.summary: Four ways rare can read (uncommon, seldom seen by one watcher, unusual in form, fleeting); each cloud form comes with its conditions, its season and its light, and a haiku can draw on any of them.

formula.full: A spread to draw from, in any mix: a rare cloud form and its conditions; the moment or light it shows in; a concrete image seen now; a season, in a word or in the image; a cut, marked or implied; a count, loose or 5-7-5. Each ingredient can be left out or doubled.
formula.essential: a rare cloud's conditions, and one thing seen now

angles.text: A lens that holds its place over a ridge while the air runs through it; the stillness is the rarity.
A sketch from life with no commentary: the cloud, the place, the time, and then the poem stops.
The cloud is common in its kind; the rarity is the one who looked up at the right minute, in a sky they know.
A sheen on a thin veil at dusk: the colour is the event, and the cloud is nearly gone without it.

llm_brief.text:
On the table: a haiku about rare clouds, from the user's words. Rare can read as uncommon in occurrence, seldom seen by one watcher, unusual in form, fleeting, or precious. Forms, each with its conditions: nacreous (very cold polar winter air; colour at twilight, when the low sun lights it from below the horizon); noctilucent (ice high in the mesosphere, lit after dark in high-latitude summer); lenticular (a still lens over a ridge while the air moves through it); Kelvin-Helmholtz (evenly spaced curls where two layers slide past each other); mammatus (pouches under a storm's anvil, still for minutes); pileus (a cap on a fast-growing cumulus top). In English a haiku can hold a concrete image seen now, a cut between two parts (a dash, a colon or a line break, since English has no kireji), and a season in a word or in the image. Exemplars: Issa's plain sky named in full; Basho's cloud that reads as a forecast; Basho's cloudbank that breaks and opens the view.
Ways in: the twilight colour; the lens that holds still in the wind; the watcher's first sky; the plain sketch from life, where the poem stops at the image.
Dials: the count runs from 5-7-5 syllables, through three measures of about eight beats, to a loose 12 to 17 syllables; the cut runs from a dash inside a line, through a colon, to a line break between two images; the season sits in a word at the head, or in the image alone; the sighting is one haiku, or a sequence of three to five through a season.
Worn paths: ethereal, whisper, dance and tapestry for the cloud, instead the cloud holding its shape or its curls rolling along one layer; smoke for the cloud, instead ice at altitude, or water stacked over a ridge; silver lining or life lesson at the close, instead the image as the last line; rhyme at the line end, instead a sound repeated inside a line, or no rhyme; rare said outright or as expensive, instead the rarity shown in the sky, a lens that holds still or a sheen at dusk.
Open: the language (English, the prompt's language, if a default is needed); the count convention and the number of haiku stay open, and the readings and dials carry both.

ak-noise-ethereal.text: Default poetic filler for any cloud; names no shape, light or place.

ak-noise-whisper.text: Gives the cloud a voice it does not have; the sky is silent in the image.

ak-noise-silver-lining.text: A stock consolation phrase; it turns the image into a moral.

ak-noise-tapestry.text: A grand word for the sky that the three lines cannot carry.

ak-moral-last-line.instead: end on the image: the lens still over the ridge, or the last cirrus gone from the blue
ak-moral-last-line.text: A moral in the last line closes the poem early and gives the reader nothing to make.

ak-rare-named-in-poem.instead: the rarity shown in the sky: a lens that holds still in wind, or a sheen at dusk
ak-rare-named-in-poem.text: The poem names the cloud rare instead of showing the thing that makes it rare.

ak-form-forced-rhyme.instead: a sound repeated inside a line, or no rhyme at all; the cut carries the music
ak-form-forced-rhyme.text: A forced rhyme at the line end pushes the last line toward a neat finish and away from the image.

ak-rare-expensive.excluded_sense: rare as a collectible good, or rare as undercooked meat
ak-rare-expensive.instead: uncommon in occurrence in the sky, seldom seen by one watcher, unusual in form, fleeting, or held precious

ak-noise-dance.instead: the cloud holds its shape, or its curls roll along one layer
ak-noise-dance.text: Animates the cloud by habit. Both a still form and a rolling one are in the pool, as in Kelvin-Helmholtz.

ak-cloud-as-smoke.instead: ice at altitude: a pale veil of crystals, or water cloud stacked over a ridge
ak-cloud-as-smoke.text: Reads the cloud as smoke, dust or data rather than as water or ice in the sky.

k-subject-cloud.text: Does the image show the cloud, or the cloud's presence through a watcher who is looking?

test.spec: the cloud is in the image, or the watcher stops for it

k-rare-reading.text: Which reading of rare does the image carry: uncommon, seldom seen by one watcher, unusual in form, or fleeting?

test.spec: the poem's image shows one of the four readings

k-form-conditions.text: Do the conditions in the poem (cold air, a ridge, a shear layer, a storm base, a window of light) match the form it names?

test.spec: the named form and its condition agree

k-three-lines.text: Is the poem three lines or phrases, with the break between them doing work?

k-count.text: Does the count hold under the convention chosen, without filler words padding a line?

test.spec: syllables per line under the chosen convention

k-cut.text: Is there one cut between two parts, marked by a dash, a colon or a line break?

test.spec: one cut mark, with a part on each side

k-present-image.text: Are the poem's images one or two, concrete, seen now, with no feeling named and no lesson drawn?

test.spec: one or two present-tense concrete images

k-season.text: Is a season carried, by a season word or by the image?

test.spec: a season word or a season-bearing image is present

k-worn-words.text: Does any worn cloud word appear in the draft?

k-smoke-word.text: Does the cloud read as smoke, dust or data rather than as a cloud?

k-rarity-said.text: Does the poem name its rarity in a word, or let the image show it?

test.spec: rarity is shown by the sky, not announced

k-end-on-image.text: Does the last line end on the image, or add a moral?

test.spec: the final line is the image, with no lesson

k-form-conditions-watcher.text: Is it clear whether the rarity comes from the cloud's look or from the watcher's situation?

test.spec: one of the two sources is clear

q-language.text: Which language is the haiku in?
q-language.default: English, since the prompt is in English

q-count.text: Which count convention, and how many haiku?
q-count.impact: the frame and the line lengths
q-count.resolve: left open: the readings and dials in the exports carry both

prompt._about: The user's words, verbatim, as anchors.

rare_clouds._about: Rare cloud forms as they look, when they show, and what 'rare' can mean for each. Options side by side; the consumer picks. Built on the research entries (rc-*); no single cloud is chosen for the poem.

exemplars._about: One exemplar per reading, illustrative only: subjects to write toward, not lines to copy. Mixes a famous form with a deep cut.

ex-one-watcher-porch.term: a single lens over one local peak, seen from a back step
ex-one-watcher-porch.text: The first lens the watcher has seen above their own valley.

ex-unusual-fuji-cap.term: a lenticular cap on a single snowy peak
ex-unusual-fuji-cap.text: A cloud that stays on the peak while the wind goes through it.

rc-primer-classification.text: Clouds sort by altitude tier and by form; the rare forms sit in the very high (stratospheric) and extreme (mesospheric) tiers, with the troposphere holding the common ones.
behaviors: A cloud's height above the ground tells you which layer of air it is in before you see its shape
rc-primer-classification.principle: Altitude sets which cloud types can form at all.
signals: polar stratospheric or polar mesospheric label

rc-primer-optics.text: Nacreous clouds show iridescent colour, from light scattered by very small, evenly sized particles; the colour is strongest at low sun angles.
behaviors: Colour fades as the sun drops further below the horizon
Colours are most visible at low angles of sun
rc-primer-optics.principle: Colour comes from the particles and the angle of light, not from the cloud's substance.
signals: colour sheen on a thin cloud

rc-nacreous.text: A thin, iridescent cloud in the lower stratosphere that forms only in very cold polar winter air and is seen mostly around twilight.
behaviors: It forms only when temperatures fall very low, so it appears in polar winter
Mountain lee waves can cool the air enough to make lens-shaped ones
rc-nacreous.principle: Stratospheric cold makes the cloud; twilight light makes it visible.

rc-noctilucent.text: A pale silver-blue cloud of ice crystals in the mesosphere, seen after sunset in summer near each pole, roughly 80 km up (search snippet, to check); visible for a short window.
behaviors: Its height keeps it lit after the ground is dark
The season turns on and off with temperature
rc-noctilucent.principle: The cloud is high enough to catch sunlight after the ground is dark.

rc-lenticular.text: A lens-shaped cloud that stays still while air flows through it, formed on the crest of a standing wave downwind of a mountain or ridge.
behaviors: Air passes through the cloud while the cloud stays in place
Long strings form on successive wave crests
rc-lenticular.principle: The cloud marks where moist air rises and condenses on each wave, not where the air is going.
signals: cloud that does not drift against the wind
stacked smooth lenses above a ridge

rc-kelvin-helmholtz.text: A billowing, evenly spaced row of rolling curls where two air layers slide past each other at different speeds; it rolls rather than holds still.
behaviors: Upper winds faster than lower winds roll the layer into curls
The pattern moves along the shear layer
rc-kelvin-helmholtz.principle: Shear between air layers makes the waves; the cloud shows the wave.

rc-mammatus.text: Pouch-like lobes hanging under a cloud base, most often a cumulonimbus anvil, and a sign of a strong storm; lobes can stay still for minutes.
behaviors: Lobes cluster into fields that can span hundreds of kilometres
Strong storms and turbulence often sit near them
rc-mammatus.principle: Mammatus shows the base of a storm, not the storm's centre.
signals: shape that stays put while the sky moves

rcf-nacreous.text: A thin veil whose colour shows only at twilight, when low sun lights it from below the horizon.
behaviors: The colour brightens and fades within the twilight window
The sheen is the image; the cloud itself is nearly invisible without it
rcf-nacreous.principle: Rarity here is optical and seasonal: cold air and low sun must meet.

rcf-noctilucent.text: Silver-blue streaks that stay lit after the ground has gone dark, visible in high-latitude summer evenings.
behaviors: It is seen only in a short window after dusk
Its season is summer at the pole, not the local season
rcf-noctilucent.principle: Rarity is seasonal and height-bound: a cloud too high for the dark to hide it.
signals: pale blue-white in a dark sky

rcf-lenticular.text: A smooth lens or saucer that holds its place above a ridge while the wind moves through it.
behaviors: Air moves through while the shape stays put
Stacked lenses sit in a row over the peak
rcf-lenticular.principle: Rarity is in the shape and in the stillness against the wind.

rcf-kelvin-helmholtz.text: A row of evenly spaced curls rolling along a layer where two winds pass at different speeds.
behaviors: The curls move along the layer, unlike a lenticular
The pattern lasts minutes before the shear breaks it
rcf-kelvin-helmholtz.principle: Rarity is brief: the shear makes the curls and then undoes them.
signals: rolling bands in a clear sky

rcf-mammatus.text: Pouches hanging from the base of a storm cloud, clustered and still for minutes.
behaviors: The lobes keep their place while the sky moves around them
They mark the base of a storm, not its centre
rcf-mammatus.principle: Rarity is in the shape under the storm; the watcher sees the storm's underside.
signals: a field of pouches that stays put

rcf-pyrocumulus.term: pyrocumulus, a cloud grown over a fire
rcf-pyrocumulus.text: A cumulus built by a fire's heat, with smoke carried up its column. The cloud is water; the smoke is what the heat lifts. Lead only, not fetched from a source.
behaviors: The fire's updraft builds the cloud faster than the weather would
The smoke feeds the rise, and the cloud underneath is still water or ice
rcf-pyrocumulus.principle: Rarity here is in the source: a fire's heat builds a cloud the weather did not make.
signals: a column rising from a fire

rcf-pileus.term: pileus cap, seen on a tower
rcf-pileus.text: A smooth cap sitting on top of a growing cumulus, pushed up by fast rising air. From a secondary source only: check before relying on it.
behaviors: The cap forms only while the tower is still growing
It shows a rising column before any rain
rcf-pileus.principle: Rarity is in the moment of growth; the cap goes when the tower stops rising.

options: optical: pastel sheen, cold air, low sun (rcf-nacreous)
altitude or wave: lens or billows over a ridge or shear (rcf-lenticular, rcf-kelvin-helmholtz)
season-bound: summer evening at the pole (rcf-noctilucent)
shape-bound: the cloud's form, under a storm or on a tower (rcf-mammatus, rcf-pileus)
dp-rarity-source.tradeoffs: Season-bound ties most cleanly to a season word; shape-bound needs the image to carry the name, not the name carrying the image.

dp-rarity-where.term: rarity in the image or in the watcher
options: rarity shows in the cloud's look (a lens, a sheen)
rarity shows in the watcher's situation (first time, one sky)
dp-rarity-where.tradeoffs: Image-led reads stay concrete; watcher-led reads carry more feeling and more risk of telling instead of showing.

options: one sighting in one haiku: the single-poem reading of the task; it fits fleeting and seldom-seen
a sequence of three to five haiku through a season: a reading for the whole job, not the default for it; it fits uncommon-in-occurrence and season words
dp-one-or-sequence.tradeoffs: One sighting holds the image tight. A sequence can show the wait that makes a form rare, but it stretches a job that asked for one haiku into several.

rc-attention-only.term: rarity in the watcher's attention, cloud unnamed
rc-attention-only.text: The cloud is present only through the watcher's attention: the rarity sits in the looking, and the sky may show nothing the reader can name.
behaviors: The poem works through what the watcher stops for, so the cloud can stay offstage
A cloud present only as a waiting presence asks the image to carry the wait
rc-attention-only.principle: Rarity of attention is a reading of the moment, not a claim about the cloud's form.
signals: the watcher stops, not the cloud
no cloud noun in the poem
a pause in the first two lines

rc-quality-rare.text: Five readings of rare, side by side: uncommon, seldom seen by one watcher, unusual in form, fleeting, precious. The image shows which.

readings.in_practice: the form seldom forms; Kelvin-Helmholtz is called extremely rare
common elsewhere, rare in this sky
a shape the sky seldom makes; lenticular clouds were mistaken for UFOs
brief; nacreous colour lasts one twilight
valued because seldom had; the poem gives the cloud the weight of a gift

rc-quality-rare.principle: Each reading is a way the word can be heard; the image shows which.

haiku_form._about: The form of the poem: three lines, one concrete image seen now, one cut between two parts, and a season carried by a season word or by the image. Derived from the research entries (builds_on). Options are choices, not requirements.

options._about: options, not requirements: counting conventions a builder can choose from; each changes what the poem does

opt-count-575.text: The familiar frame of 5, 7 and 5 syllables. Easy to recognize; it can pad lines with filler words to hit the count.

opt-count-beats.text: Three lines of about eight beats each, keeping rhythm without counting syllables. Lines can run long or short and still hold the breath.

opt-count-loose.text: Short uneven lines near 12 to 17 syllables that read as one breath and lean on the image rather than the number.

opt-count-monoku.text: The whole poem in one line, with no line break, so the cut takes a dash or colon. Compresses the image into one breath.

hf-form.text: Three phrases, traditionally 17 on in a 5-7-5 pattern, focused on nature and seasonal change through imagistic language.
behaviors: The count is a frame the poem fills, not a rule every English poem keeps
hf-form.principle: The short form asks one image to carry the whole poem.
signals: a nature image in the first two lines

hf-kigo.text: A season word anchors the poem in a time of year; Japanese kigo carry centuries of meaning, and English ones vary by region.
behaviors: A season word that means little to the reader needs the image to supply the season
hf-kigo.principle: The season word places the poem in time through shared association.
signals: a word naming a season or a seasonal phenomenon
an image that shows the season without naming it

hf-cut.text: Cutting a haiku creates a juxtaposition between images, ideas or moments, and the two parts spark against each other.
behaviors: Two images set side by side make the reader supply the link
The cut can fall after the image, after the season word, or between two images
hf-cut.principle: Tension between two parts gives a short poem its depth.
signals: a dash, colon or line break separating two images
the two parts share no explicit connective

hf-disjunction.text: Gilbert's view: in English haiku the force of disjunction, not juxtaposition alone, supplies the creative tension.
behaviors: A pair of images that do not obviously connect asks the reader to make the connection
hf-disjunction.principle: Brevity makes disjunction work harder than in longer poems.
signals: two parts with no stated link

hf-sky-words.text: Plain sky and weather words the translated haiku use: sky plainly named, cloudbanks, moonlight, rain and snow.
signals: a single cloud form instead of a general sky

hf-worn-words.term: worn words for clouds and sky
hf-worn-words.text: Words that show up in weak English haiku about clouds: they give the cloud a human act or a vague mood.
behaviors: A cloud given a human verb draws attention to the poet, not the cloud
hf-worn-words.principle: A specific cloud shape or light change does what these words only gesture at.
signals: a last line that explains what the cloud means

hfm-kigo.text: The season is placed either by naming it with a season word or by an image that shows it; English practice mixes the two, and the choice is the poem's.
behaviors: An image that only shows the season leaves the naming to the reader
A season word beside a weak image adds a label without a picture
hfm-kigo.principle: A season word places the poem in time; the image can do the same job without the word.
signals: a seasonal phenomenon with no season's name

hfm-juxtaposition.text: Two images sit side by side with no stated link; the reader supplies the connection, and that gap is the poem's tension.
behaviors: Two images sharing a quality such as light, cold or motion link faster than unrelated ones
A connective such as because or like closes the gap and flattens the poem
hfm-juxtaposition.principle: The poem lives in the space between the two parts, so the parts should not explain each other.
signals: no because, like or as joining the parts
two concrete nouns on either side of the cut

hf-present-image.text: One concrete thing seen now, with the poem naming no feeling and drawing no lesson.
behaviors: A last line that stays an image leaves the reader to make the feeling
A last line that states the meaning closes the poem early
A present-tense verb keeps the cloud moving in the reader's sight
hf-present-image.principle: The reader makes the feeling from what is shown.
signals: no abstraction in the last line
one sensory detail per line at most
last line made of nouns and light

hfm-cut-english.term: the cut in English (dash, colon, line break)
hfm-cut-english.text: English has no kireji, so the cut is marked by a dash, a colon, an ellipsis or a line break; each mark sets the break at a different weight.
behaviors: A dash keeps the two parts in one breath
A colon points forward, so the second part reads as the consequence of the first
A line break gives the cut silence and needs no mark
A line break placed before the final image can act as the cut
hfm-cut-english.principle: The mark sets how hard the two parts strike against each other.
signals: a line break with no mark between two images

hf-count-english.text: English has no equal of the on, so the count is open. 5-7-5 is one practice among several; the Japanese on (17 on, the traditional frame) does not map to 17 syllables.
behaviors: 5-7-5 keeps a familiar shape and can pad lines with filler words
Three measures of about eight beats keep the rhythm without counting syllables
A loose count of about 12 to 17 syllables reads as one breath and leans on the image
A one-line monoku drops the line break and lets the cut carry the rhythm
The on is a sound unit, so 17 on does not map to 17 syllables
hf-count-english.principle: Each count convention changes what the poem does; the choice belongs to the poem.
signals: a count that differs without losing the image
a count that checks out while a line pads

inv-haiku-form.text: Three lines, a concrete image seen now, one cut between two parts, and a season carried by a season word or by the image.
invariant: a season carried in the poem
variable: image count (one, two or more; left open)
behaviors: A short last line lands harder than a long one, so the image arrives last
The break before the last line works as a pause before the turn
inv-haiku-form.principle: The frame stays fixed while the count, the cut mark and the image count change, and the form still holds.

exemplars._about: Haiku about sky, cloud, rain or weather, quoted from a fetched translation page. What transfers is a move, not a motif.

ex-basho-snow.text: The cloud reads as a forecast: the sky's shape points to snow not yet fallen, and the cut sits between the sky and the weather.
ex-basho-snow.poem: Crossing half the sky, on my way to the capital, big clouds promise snow
ex-basho-snow.transfers: a cloud as sign of the next weather
ex-basho-snow.does_not_transfer: the snow itself as a motif

ex-basho-cloudbank.text: The cloud breaks apart and the view opens; the rarity is a gap that reveals the landscape.
ex-basho-cloudbank.poem: Black Cloudbank Broken Scatters in the night...Now see Moon-lighted mountains!
ex-basho-cloudbank.transfers: a moving cloud subtracted to reveal a view

ex-issa-new-year.term: the new year and a deep blue sky
ex-issa-new-year.text: The sky is the entire image, named plainly; the weight sits in the stated simplicity, not in any effect.
ex-issa-new-year.poem: The new year arrived in utter simplicity - and a deep blue sky
ex-issa-new-year.transfers: plain sky as the whole picture

ex-buson-rain.text: Weather is the ground for an unnamed feeling; the poem never names the feeling, only where it sits.
ex-buson-rain.poem: In seasonal rain along a nameless river fear too has no name
ex-buson-rain.transfers: a weather condition paired with a feeling left unnamed

lines._about: Season words, image pools, sensory words and cut placement for a haiku about one rare cloud sighting. Options side by side; the consumer picks.

kigo._about: One season word per rare form. Season words not in a source are inferred.

ls-kigo-nacreous.text: Several season words fit, each placing the sighting a different way. None of them is sourced as a season word.
behaviors: Midwinter points to the coldest air, the condition that forms the cloud
Winter dusk points to the twilight window in which the colour shows
Early spring dusk places the sighting late in the polar season
ls-kigo-nacreous.principle: Season words place the cloud in the cold and the light the form needs.
signals: pale sheen in a winter sky

ls-kigo-noctilucent.text: Several summer words fit. Each one points at a different part of the light that keeps the cloud visible after dark.
behaviors: Midsummer places the sighting in the season the high air is warm enough
Summer dusk pulls the reader into a long evening before the streaks appear
White night names the light that never fully goes, so the sky stays lit
ls-kigo-noctilucent.principle: Summer places the sighting, and the light of the season places the cloud after dark.

ls-kigo-lenticular.text: Several wind words fit, from different seasons. No fetched source names a season for this cloud.
behaviors: Autumn wind points to the strong ridge winds of the turning year
Early winter wind places the sighting in the first cold air over the peaks
Spring wind points to a milder ridge with the same stationary cloud
ls-kigo-lenticular.principle: Ridge wind is the condition; the season word names which winds the reader hears.
signals: a ridge in the first two lines

ls-kigo-kelvin-helmholtz.text: Several wind words fit, one for each season of shear. No fetched source names a season for this cloud.
behaviors: Spring and thaw wind point to layers of air sliding over one another in the first warm days
Summer squall places the shear at the front of a gust
Autumn gale points to strong shear over open country
ls-kigo-kelvin-helmholtz.principle: Shear between layers is the condition; a wind word tells the reader the layers are moving.
signals: rolling bands in a windy sky

ls-kigo-mammatus.text: Several storm words fit, from different seasons. The lobes hang under a storm cloud whatever the month; the season is inferred.
behaviors: Summer storm places the lobes under a thunderhead in its warmest season
Thunderstorm names the anvil the lobes hang from
Autumn storm points to a cold-front storm with the same underside
ls-kigo-mammatus.principle: Mammatus sits under a storm base, so a storm word places it.

ls-kigo-pileus.text: Several afternoon words fit, from different seasons. No fetched source names a season, so treat them as leads.
behaviors: Summer afternoon points to the surface heat that drives a fast updraft
Spring heat places the cap in a warm afternoon after a cold morning
Early autumn afternoon points to the same updraft in cooler air
ls-kigo-pileus.principle: A fast updraft needs surface heat, so the afternoon word places the cap.

images._about: Image pools by job: light on the cloud, the cloud's motion or stillness, the watcher's place. Each candidate is an exemplar labeled by the form it serves.

ls-img-light-nacreous.text: Mother-of-pearl tints at twilight, when the sun is 1 to 6 degrees below the horizon.

ls-img-light-noctilucent.text: Pale streaks still lit after the ground has gone dark, as the sun sits below the horizon.

ls-img-motion-lenticular.text: Lens-shaped cloud that does not drift against the wind, stacked above a ridge.

ls-img-motion-mammatus.text: Lobes that stay visibly static for ten to fifteen minutes while the sky moves around them.

ls-img-motion-kelvin-helmholtz.text: A row of rolling billows that moves along one layer, the shape change is the whole image.

ls-img-watch-ufo.term: lens cloud taken for a craft
ls-img-watch-ufo.text: A watcher who mistakes the still lens for something that flies: rarity as misreading.

ls-img-watch-attention.term: a cold cup on the sill, the watcher still at the glass
ls-img-watch-attention.text: The cloud is not named. The image is the watcher at the window, the cup going cold while the sky changes behind the glass.

decision._about: Where the cut falls, and what each placement does to the reading. Options, not requirements.

ls-cut-after-image.text: Image first, then a break; the season word follows and the reader links them. The reading is the cloud as seen, with the season left implicit.

ls-cut-after-season.text: Season word first, then a break and the image. The reading is the season setting the scene before the cloud arrives.

ls-cut-between-images.text: Two images side by side with a break between them; the reader supplies the link. The reading is disjunction, the rarity in the gap.

ls-sensory.text: Colour, light and temperature words are sourced; sound words are inferred and none is sourced.
behaviors: A cold word next to a colour word tells the reader the cloud is far up
ls-sensory.principle: Light and cold are the sourced senses; sound is left to the image.

lexicon._about: Brain-dump vocabulary for a rare-clouds haiku. Seed material at tier 2 to 4: it widens the search, it does not define the task. Deep cuts are marked by the word 'deep cut' in text.

lex-cloud-descriptors.text: Human words for cloud looks, from everyday to unusual.
properties: shape words: pouch, lens, cap, billow, fleece, anvil
light words: sheen, rim, glow from under, backlit edge
motion words: hangs, holds, unspools, fraying, tearing

lex-haiku-associations.text: Haiku-world words and less-said associations. Deep cut: Shiki's shasei (sketch from life) and Basho's karumi (lightness) suit a plain cloud image better than the Western sublime.
behaviors: A sketch from life gives the cloud a place and a time and then stops

lex-cloud-metaphors-moods.text: Metaphors and moods to test against a draft; a lead, not a fact. Deep cut: Luke Howard's naming (cirrus, cumulus, stratus) turned cloud into a language of tiers.
keywords: a sheet hung out to dry
properties: metaphor sources: weaving, paper, glass, breath, hunting

taxonomy._about: Keyword registers. One group per register; each entry holds a keyword list for search and indexing.

influences._about: Traditions and people with what each contributes. Contributions, never a style to copy.
